import importlib.util, shutil
for m in ['pypdf', 'pdfplumber', 'fitz', 'pypdfium2', 'PIL']:
 print(m, bool(importlib.util.find_spec(m)))
for b in ['pdftoppm', 'pdfinfo', 'gs', 'python3']:
 print(b, shutil.which(b))

/bin/bash -c "mkdir -p tmp/pdfs && python3 - <<'PY'
from pypdf import PdfReader
from pathlib import Path
r=PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')
print('Pages:',len(r.pages))
print('Metadata:',r.metadata)
with Path('tmp/pdfs/manuscript.txt').open('w') as f:
 for i,p in enumerate(r.pages):
  f.write(f'\\n\\n===== PAGE {i+1} =====\\n\\n')
  f.write(p.extract_text(extraction_mode='layout'))
print(Path('tmp/pdfs/manuscript.txt').read_text()[:48000])
PY"

strengths: The task is well motivated: combining a reference person image with a relative description addresses limitations of either modality alone. ITCPR provides a useful evaluation resource with 2,202 queries and a 20,510-image gallery drawn from three datasets.

The framework is simple and practical. It adapts CLIP using existing person image-caption data, then trains a shallow inversion network without CPR training triplets. The pipeline figures and implementation details make the overall approach understandable.

The improvements over simple baselines using the same adapted encoders are substantial. In Table 1, the ViT-L/14 text-supervised TINet achieves 45.549% Rank-1 and 55.260% mAP, compared with 32.016% and 41.831% for image-text feature averaging.

The appendix provides useful additional evidence, including data-volume experiments, runtime measurements, and loss comparisons. Table B shows approximately 3.1–3.4 percentage-point Rank-1 improvements from CMPM over ITC. The acknowledged limitation concerning facial and body consistency is also helpful.
weaknesses: The comparison with the closest methods does not adequately isolate the contribution. Pic2Word and SEARLE retain inversion networks trained with the original CLIP encoders, including when evaluated with fine-tuned encoders; Table 1 explicitly acknowledges this mismatch. Retraining these methods with the same adapted encoders and person data is necessary to establish the claimed advantage. Table B partially addresses this concern, but does not replace those matched comparisons.

The evaluation lacks a clearly independent model-selection protocol. ITCPR is described as exclusively for testing, yet Section 5.3 selects network depth, width, prompt, and token count using the reported retrieval performance. No separate CPR validation split is described. This apparent test-set tuning undermines confidence in generalization and requires clarification or evaluation on an untouched test partition.

Methodological originality is limited beyond the task and benchmark: the framework combines established person-retrieval fine-tuning, image-to-token inversion, and CMPM supervision. These adaptations can be useful, but the paper needs a sharper account of the new insight beyond combining existing components. The explanation that text supervision reduces background dependence rests mainly on a few qualitative examples.

Benchmark reliability is insufficiently documented. Appendix B.1 mines additional positives using an unspecified visual encoder followed by manual verification, without reporting retrieval depth, annotation agreement, or an audit of missed positives. These details matter for mAP. Results separated by source dataset and extent of clothing change would also clarify the benchmark's coverage.

Some reporting ambiguities hinder reproducibility and interpretation. Table 1 labels configurations with a sum of losses, while Appendix C.4 describes fusion of separately trained TINets; this distinction should be explicit. No repeated-run variability or confidence intervals support the smaller prompt and fusion improvements.

The proposed application enables person tracking across clothing changes, but the manuscript does not discuss privacy, misidentification, or misuse risks, or document permitted reuse and redistribution of the source imagery. The planned benchmark release needs an explicit account of these considerations.
